# Dot plots {#sec-dot-plots} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_blockbuster()` Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_blockbuster()`, modeled on a Blockbuster Video store: royal blue background, yellow ticket stub marks, white Arial text, and an Impact title. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false} ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** :::
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dot_plots_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: :::: ## Description A dot plot shows each number in the data as a dot along one axis. It helps us see where the numbers come together, where there are none, and which numbers are far from the rest,[^patterns] as long as there are not too many numbers.[^data-size] Each dot stands for one row in the data.[^observation] A pile is a set of dots, one on top of the next. The piles stand over groups[^categories] or along a number line. In `ggplot2`, we can make dot plots with [`geom_dotplot()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_dotplot.html) ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: [Blockbuster Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster_(retailer)) was a group of stores where people paid to take out movies, watch them at home, and bring them back a few days later.[^rent] In the last few years before 2000, the end of most work weeks started at Blockbuster Video. ::: {.column-margin} ![Blockbuster Video membership card (source: Wikipedia)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/56/Blockbuster_membership_card.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled){fig-align="center" width="50%" height="50%"} ::: We'll make up[^simulate] how many movies 60 homes[^household] took out in one week with `rpois()`, which picks whole numbers (0, 1, 2, and so on).[^rpois] Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 60 homes every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1993) # same 60 households every time the code runs blockbuster_rentals <- tibble( household_id = 1:60, # 60 different households, one row each rentals = rpois(n = 60, lambda = 3) # weekly rentals (about 3 on average) ) glimpse(blockbuster_rentals) #> Rows: 60 #> Columns: 2 #> $ household_id 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, … #> $ rentals 2, 0, 2, 4, 3, 3, 2, 2, 5, … ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution The number of movies a home takes out is a whole number:[^counts] a home takes out 0, 1, 2, or more movies, but never 2.5. A dot plot is a good way to show numbers like these because each dot is one home, so the graph is just the data put into piles. ![A Blockbuster store in Durham, North Carolina (source: Wikipedia)](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/2008-09-24_Blockbuster_in_Durham.jpg/3840px-2008-09-24_Blockbuster_in_Durham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=thumbnail){fig-align="center" width="80%" height="80%"} Because we picked how many movies a home takes out on average in `rpois()`,[^rate] we know what the piles should look like before we make the graph. Below we'll move from the numbers, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula] ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first ten homes. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(blockbuster_rentals$rentals, 10) #> [1] 2 0 2 4 3 3 2 2 5 0 ``` ::: ::: Most of these homes took out two or three movies, two took out none, and one took out five. If we find how many of all 60 homes are in each pile, we can compare each pile to the number of homes we'd expect[^expected] (we'll see where `dpois()` comes from below). ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} blockbuster_rentals |> count(rentals) |> mutate(expected = round(60 * dpois(rentals, lambda = 3), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: The piles we got stay close to the ones we expected. The variance is a number for how far the numbers fall from the mean.[^variance] Numbers like these have one more thing worth looking at: the mean and the variance should be about the same. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} blockbuster_rentals |> summarise(mean = mean(rentals), variance = var(rentals)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The dot plot below puts one dot for each home over the number of movies it took out. The highest piles stand at two and three movies, and the piles get lower on both sides. The broken line marks the rate we used in `rpois()` (3 a week). The right side runs out farther than the left because a home can't take out fewer than 0 movies.[^skew] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals, aes(x = rentals)) + geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.3) + geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = "dashed", color = "white") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:7) + labs(x = "Number of rentals") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dot_plots_files/figure-html/draw_dotplot-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: We can write the `rpois()` code that made the data as one short line:[^notation] $$ X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 3) $$ This line names [a rule for how many times something happens at a set rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution) in a set time (here, movies taken out in one week).[^poisson] The rule has only one number in it,[^parameter] the rate ($\lambda$), and that number is both the mean and the variance. That's why the mean (2.9) and variance (2.8) of the data we made up are so close. The chance that a home takes out just $k$ movies is:[^pmf] $$ P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!} $$ This is what `dpois()` works out. For $k = 3$, $P(X = 3) = 3^3 e^{-3} / 3! \approx 0.224$, so we'd expect about $60 \times 0.224 \approx 13$ of our 60 homes to take out three movies. We got 15. Try a larger `lambda` in `rpois()` and the piles move right and get wider, because the mean and the variance grow together. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: 1. Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()` 2. Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data` 3. Put `rentals` on the `x` axis[^map] 4. Add `geom_dotplot()` on top[^layer] 5. Set `binwidth` to `1` (one pile for each number of movies)[^binwidth] and change the `dotsize`[^dotsize] 6. Put a mark on the `x` axis at each whole number from 0 to 7 with `scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:7)`[^breaks] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_dotplot <- labs( title = "Blockbuster Video", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Rentals per household in one week", x = "Number of rentals") ggp2_dotplot <- ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals, aes(x = rentals)) + geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:7) ggp2_dotplot + labs_dotplot ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dot_plots_files/figure-html/create_graph_dotplot-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: One problem with a dot plot is that the numbers on the `y` axis don't mean anything.[^dot-y-axis] The axis says `count`, but its numbers run from 0 to 1, even though the highest pile in our graph holds 15 homes. These numbers don't match the piles because `geom_dotplot()` doesn't set how high a pile stands by the number of homes in it.[^y-scale] It makes each dot a part of the `binwidth` on the `x` axis (one movie) as wide, and `dotsize` sets how big that part is,[^dot-width] then puts the dots one on top of the next until the pile runs out. How high a pile stands comes from how many dots it holds *and* how big each dot is, so changing `dotsize` makes every pile higher or lower without changing the data. The `y` axis isn't showing a number of anything; it's just space left over to hold the dots. The number of homes is still in the graph, but we find it by adding up the dots in each pile, not by looking across to the axis. Because the axis can lead people to the wrong number, it's common to take the `y` axis off with `scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)`. ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} labs_dotplot <- labs( title = "Blockbuster Video", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Rentals per household in one week", x = "Number of rentals") ggp2_dotplot <- ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals, aes(x = rentals)) + geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.2) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:7) + scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) ggp2_dotplot + labs_dotplot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](dot_plots_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: [^dot-y-axis]: Read more in the [function reference.](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_dotplot.html#details) [^patterns]: Patterns, gaps, and outliers. [^data-size]: Small to moderate datasets. [^observation]: Each dot represents one observation. [^categories]: Dots can be stacked over categories. [^packages]: Install and load the packages. [^rent]: Rent. [^simulate]: Simulate. [^household]: A household. [^rpois]: `rpois()` draws random counts from a Poisson distribution. [^seed]: Setting the random seed. [^counts]: Count data: non-negative integers. [^rate]: The rental rate, which is the Poisson parameter $\lambda$ (`lambda = 3`). [^formula]: The formula. [^expected]: The expected count for each value, $60 \times$ `dpois()`. [^variance]: The variance: the average squared distance from the mean (`var()`). [^skew]: The distribution is right skewed, because counts are bounded below by zero. [^notation]: A single statement in distribution notation: $X$ is distributed as Poisson with rate $\lambda = 3$. [^poisson]: The Poisson distribution, which describes counts of events in a fixed window of time. [^parameter]: A single parameter. [^pmf]: The probability mass function of the Poisson distribution. [^labels]: The labels (title, subtitle, caption, and axis titles). [^map]: Map `rentals` to `x` in `aes()`. [^layer]: Add the `geom_dotplot()` layer. [^binwidth]: The bin width. With `binwidth = 1`, each bin holds one count. [^dotsize]: Adjust the `dotsize` argument, the dot diameter relative to `binwidth`. [^breaks]: Axis breaks: tick marks and labels at each integer from 0 to 7. [^y-scale]: `geom_dotplot()` does not stack dots in count units on the `y` axis. [^dot-width]: Dot diameter is `binwidth` × `dotsize` (here 1 × 0.2, so each dot is a fifth of a bin wide).
